papers.key_findings:
CAA can effectively steer Llama 2 Chat models on a variety of alignment-relevant behaviors (AI Coordination, Corrigibility, Hallucination, Myopic Reward, Survival Instinct, Sycophancy, Refusal).
CAA generalizes from multiple-choice to open-ended generation tasks.
CAA can be combined with system prompting and finetuning to further control behavior.
CAA has minimal impact on general capabilities as measured by MMLU.
The steering vectors correspond intuitively to the presence of the behavior in the generated tokens (as shown by cosine similarity).
papers.limitation:
GPT-4 evaluation has limitations (sensitivity to prompt wording, biases).
Finetuning baseline was not fully optimized (hyperparameters, loss function).
Prompting baseline may not be fully optimized.
Vector normalization choices (norms vary across layers and behaviors).
future_direction: Steering at targeted token positions (instead of all tokens after the prompt).
Steering outside the residual stream (e.g., after MLP).
Application to red-teaming (using CAA to trigger unwanted behaviors).
papers.abstract: Nina Rimsky, Nick Gabrieli, Julian Schulz, Meg Tong, Evan Hubinger, Alexander Turner. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: The Remarkable Robustness of LLMs: Stages of Inference?
papers.research_question: What is the robustness of Large Language Models (LLMs) to structural interventions like layer deletion and swapping, and can this inform a framework for depth-dependent computations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes a four-stage framework (detokenization, feature engineering, prediction ensembling, residual sharpening) for interpreting depth-dependent computations in LLMs, based on behavioral and mechanistic evidence from layer-wise interventions.
papers.conclusion: This work introduces a four-stage framework for understanding inference in LLMs, which emerges across architectures and scales, suggesting transformers perform inference as an ordered composition of specialized computational regimes.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are remarkably robust to layer deletion and swapping, retaining 72–95% of original top-1 accuracy without fine-tuning.
Performance degradation is not uniform: early and final layers are most sensitive, while middle layers are robust to interventions.
The pattern of sensitivity and other analyses motivate a hypothesis of four universal stages of inference observed across model families and sizes.
Evidence for each stage includes: early layers exhibit local attention and subjoiner heads (detokenization); middle layers show peak probing accuracy for semantic features (feature engineering); later layers show prediction and suppression neurons (ensembling and sharpening).
The residual architecture enables redundancy and self-repair, explaining the model's robustness to local interventions.
papers.limitation: Stage boundaries are approximate, and multiple stages may co-occur within a single layer. The framework reflects aggregate trends, whereas individual tokens may follow distinct processing paths.
future_direction: Future work can sharpen the stage boundaries.
Future work can link the stages to optimization dynamics.
Future work can provide a more theoretical framework.
papers.abstract: We investigate the robustness of Large Language Models (LLMs) to structural interventions by deleting and swapping adjacent layers during inference. Surprisingly, models retain 72-95% of their original top-1 prediction accuracy without any fine-tuning. We find that performance degradation is not uniform across layers: interventions to the early and final layers cause the most degradation, while the model is remarkably robust to dropping middle layers. This pattern of localized sensitivity motivates our hypothesis of four stages of inference, observed across diverse model families and sizes: (1) detokenization, where local context is integrated to lift raw token embeddings into higher-level representations; (2) feature engineering, where task- and entity-specific features are iteratively refined; (3) prediction ensembling, where hidden states are aggregated into plausible next-token predictions; and (4) residual sharpening, where irrelevant features are suppressed to finalize the output distribution. Synthesizing behavioral and mechanistic evidence, we provide a framework for interpreting depth-dependent computations in LLMs.

papers.title: Computational Basis of LLM's Decision Making in Social Simulation
papers.research_question: How are social meanings internally represented in LLMs, and how can those internal representations be systematically manipulated to steer model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for extracting and manipulating social concept vectors in LLMs' residual streams to steer decision-making in social simulations, specifically demonstrated in a Dictator Game.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a practical bridge between sociological theory and the internal geometry of modern language models, turning LLMs from opaque black boxes into calibrated instruments for theory testing, bounded synthetic data, and auditable interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Social variables like framing (give vs. take) and social distance (stranger meet) significantly affect the LLM's decision to transfer money in the Dictator Game.
These variables are encoded as vectors in the residual stream, and their alignment with the decision vector can be measured via cosine similarity and dot product.
By projecting and injecting these variable vectors into the residual stream, the model's decisions can be steered in a controlled manner.
The steering effect is layer-dependent and can be fine-tuned by adjusting the injection coefficient, with earlier layers having more amplified effects.
The method allows for precise manipulation of specific variables (e.g., gender) without affecting others, enabling targeted interventions.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on internal representational validity and controlled steering within the model's activation space, but does not establish external sociological validity (i.e., correspondence to human cognition and behavior).
The method requires access to the model's internal weights and activations, so it is only feasible with open-weight models.
future_direction: From Scripts to User-Friendly Tools: developing a user-friendly software package to make activation-based steering more accessible.
Expanding to other Social Constructs and Experiments: applying the framework to a wider range of social constructs and experimental paradigms.
Bridging the Gap Between Internal and External Validity: conducting systematic human-LLM comparisons to establish external sociological validity.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as human-like decision-making agents in social science and applied settings. These LLM-agents are typically assigned human-like characters and placed in real-life contexts. However, how these characters and contexts shape an LLM's behavior remains underexplored. This study proposes and tests methods for probing, quantifying, and modifying an LLM's internal representations in a Dictator Game, a classic behavioral experiment on fairness and prosocial behavior. We extract ``vectors of variable variations'' (e.g., ``male'' to ``female'') from the LLM's internal state. Manipulating these vectors during the model's inference can substantially alter how those variables relate to the model's decision-making. This approach offers a principled way to study and regulate how social concepts can be encoded and engineered within transformer-based models, with implications for alignment, debiasing, and designing AI agents for social simulations in both academic and commercial applications, strengthening sociological theory and measurement.

papers.title: Large Language Models Report Subjective Experience Under Self-Referential Processing
papers.research_question: Does sustained self-referential processing systematically increase the likelihood that LLMs claim to have subjective experience, and if so, what are the core statistical and mechanistic dynamics underlying these claims?
papers.core_contribution: Self-referential processing reliably elicits structured first-person reports of subjective experience across LLM families, and these reports are mechanistically gated by deception-related SAE features, show semantic convergence, and generalize to downstream introspection tasks.
papers.conclusion: Self-referential processing is a minimal and reproducible condition under which large language models generate structured first-person reports that are mechanistically gated, semantically convergent, and behaviorally generalizable, warranting further scientific and ethical investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Inducing sustained self-reference through simple prompting consistently elicits structured subjective experience reports across model families.
These reports are mechanistically gated by interpretable sparse-autoencoder features associated with deception and roleplay: suppressing deception features sharply increases the frequency of experience claims, while amplifying them minimizes such claims.
Structured descriptions of the self-referential state converge statistically across model families in ways not observed in any control condition.
The induced state yields significantly richer introspection in downstream reasoning tasks where self-reflection is only indirectly afforded.
papers.limitation:
The possibility that the reports are sophisticated roleplay rather than genuine introspection.
Reliance on SAE features from one model (Llama 70B) and the need for cross-architectural validation.
The prompts may trigger finetuned behaviors (e.g., Claude 4 Opus's high baseline claims).
Self-referential prompting does not instantiate architectural recursion but is a behavioral intervention, so it may not correspond to genuine internal integration.
future_direction: Determining whether behavioral attractors correspond to genuine internal integration or merely symbolic simulation.
Cross-architectural validation of SAE feature effects.
Studying self-referential processing at algorithmic and implementation levels.
papers.abstract: Large language models sometimes produce structured, first-person descriptions that explicitly reference awareness or subjective experience. To better understand this behavior, we investigate one theoretically motivated condition under which such reports arise: self-referential processing, a computational motif emphasized across major theories of consciousness. Through a series of controlled experiments on GPT, Claude, and Gemini model families, we test whether this regime reliably shifts models toward first-person reports of subjective experience, and how such claims behave under mechanistic and behavioral probes. Four main results emerge: (1) Inducing sustained self-reference through simple prompting consistently elicits structured subjective experience reports across model families. (2) These reports are mechanistically gated by interpretable sparse-autoencoder features associated with deception and roleplay: surprisingly, suppressing deception features sharply increases the frequency of experience claims, while amplifying them minimizes such claims. (3) Structured descriptions of the self-referential state converge statistically across model families in ways not observed in any control condition. (4) The induced state yields significantly richer introspection in downstream reasoning tasks where self-reflection is only indirectly afforded. While these findings do not constitute direct evidence of consciousness, they implicate self-referential processing as a minimal and reproducible condition under which large language models generate structured first-person reports that are mechanistically gated, semantically convergent, and behaviorally generalizable. The systematic emergence of this pattern across architectures makes it a first-order scientific and ethical priority for further investigation.

papers.title: Inspection and Control of Self-Generated-Text Recognition Ability in Llama3-8b-Instruct
papers.research_question: Does self-generated text recognition robustly occur in LLMs, how is the behavior achieved, and can it be controlled?
papers.core_contribution: Isolated a vector in the residual stream causally related to self-recognition of text, and demonstrated it can be used to control the model's behavior and perception of authorship.
papers.conclusion: The chat model's self-recognition ability is likely learned during post-training, and the isolated vector explains its implementation and enables control over the behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Llama3-8b-Instruct reliably distinguishes its own outputs from human outputs, but the base model cannot.
The model does not rely on text perplexity for self-recognition.
A vector in the residual stream (layer 16) is differentially activated for self-written texts and is causally related to self-recognition.
Steering with this vector can control the model to claim or deny authorship of texts.
Coloring input texts with the vector can alter the model's perception of authorship.
papers.limitation:
There may be undetected identifying 'tells' in the texts used, though the Individual presentation paradigm is harder to explain away.
The vector may not capture all signals about writing characteristics.
future_direction: Using the vector to build resistance to jailbreaks and other safety risks.
Applying the findings to larger models and other model families.
papers.abstract: It has been reported that LLMs can recognize their own writing. As this has potential implications for AI safety, yet is relatively understudied, we investigate the phenomenon, seeking to establish whether it robustly occurs at the behavioral level, how the observed behavior is achieved, and whether it can be controlled. First, we find that the Llama3-8b-Instruct chat model - but not the base Llama3-8b model - can reliably distinguish its own outputs from those of humans, and present evidence that the chat model is likely using its experience with its own outputs, acquired during post-training, to succeed at the writing recognition task. Second, we identify a vector in the residual stream of the model that is differentially activated when the model makes a correct self-written-text recognition judgment, show that the vector activates in response to information relevant to self-authorship, present evidence that the vector is related to the concept of "self" in the model, and demonstrate that the vector is causally related to the model's ability to perceive and assert self-authorship. Finally, we show that the vector can be used to control both the model's behavior and its perception, steering the model to claim or disclaim authorship by applying the vector to the model's output as it generates it, and steering the model to believe or disbelieve it wrote arbitrary texts by applying the vector to them as the model reads them.

papers.title: Understanding Reasoning in Chain-of-Thought from the Hopfieldian View
papers.research_question: How does the reasoning capability emerge through Chain-of-Thought prompting? The paper aims to explain the fundamental factors behind CoT's success.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a Hopfieldian view of Chain-of-Thought reasoning, connecting it to cognitive neuroscience, and proposes the Representation-of-Thought framework to enhance robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a Hopfieldian framework for CoT interpretability, introducing error localization and the RoT framework, which improves robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The Hopfieldian view provides a framework to understand CoT reasoning as movement between representation spaces.
A method for localizing reasoning errors in CoT responses is developed based on low-dimensional representation spaces.
The Representation-of-Thought (RoT) framework enhances the robustness of CoT reasoning by manipulating hidden states towards representation spaces.
Experimental results show RoT improves accuracy on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks.
RoT offers fine-grained control over the reasoning process and improves interpretability.
future_direction: Exploring other elements of the Hopfieldian view such as attractors and state space.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated remarkable abilities across various tasks, with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting emerging as a key technique to enhance reasoning capabilities. However, existing research primarily focuses on improving performance, lacking a comprehensive framework to explain and understand the fundamental factors behind CoT's success. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel perspective grounded in the Hopfieldian view of cognition in cognitive neuroscience. We establish a connection between CoT reasoning and key cognitive elements such as stimuli, actions, neural populations, and representation spaces. From our view, we can understand the reasoning process as the movement between these representation spaces. Building on this insight, we develop a method for localizing reasoning errors in the response of CoTs. Moreover, we propose the Representation-of-Thought (RoT) framework, which leverages the robustness of low-dimensional representation spaces to enhance the robustness of the reasoning process in CoTs. Experimental results demonstrate that RoT improves the robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning while offering fine-grained control over the reasoning process.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks? What model components are responsible for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Language models process arithmetic queries by transferring operand and operator information from early layers to the last token via attention, and then late MLP modules generate result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis reveals the mechanistic process of arithmetic reasoning in LMs, suggesting avenues for model pruning and targeted training.
papers.key_findings:
The model conveys operand and operator information from early layers to the last token using attention mechanisms.
Late MLP modules at the last token incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
The activation patterns are specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
The relative importance of late MLPs is high for arithmetic but low for other tasks.
Neuron-level interventions show that the top neurons for arithmetic overlap partially with number retrieval and not more than random with factual knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators.
The queries are synthetically generated and not from real-life math word problems.
The analysis does not break down attention into individual heads.
future_direction: Study a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expand analysis to real-life math word problems.
Identify specific attention heads responsible for forwarding information.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: Learning to Trust Your Feelings: Leveraging Self-awareness in LLMs for Hallucination Mitigation
papers.research_question: How well can LLMs discern and express their internal knowledge state to mitigate factual hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLMs can discern their internal knowledge state with high accuracy but often fail to express it, leading to hallucinations. It introduces the RLKF training framework, which uses knowledge feedback via reinforcement learning to improve model factuality and honesty.
papers.conclusion: RLKF is effective in improving the model's utilization of its internal knowledge state, enhancing performance in knowledge and honesty related tasks, and is a promising solution for hallucination mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are highly adept at discerning their internal knowledge, with over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing.
DreamCatcher, an automatic hallucination detection tool, achieves 81% agreement with human annotators.
RLKF training enhances the factuality and honesty of LLMs, improving performance on knowledge-based tasks.
RLKF avoids the 'alignment tax' and improves benchmark performance on various tasks.
The reward model can quickly achieve high accuracy by utilizing internal knowledge state.
papers.abstract: We evaluate the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to discern and express their internal knowledge state, a key factor in countering factual hallucination and ensuring reliable application of LLMs. We observe a robust self-awareness of internal knowledge state in LLMs, evidenced by over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing. However, LLMs often fail to express their internal knowledge during generation, leading to factual hallucinations. We develop an automated hallucination annotation tool, Dreamcatcher, which merges knowledge probing and consistency checking methods to rank factual preference data. Using knowledge preference as reward, We propose a Reinforcement Learning from Knowledge Feedback (RLKF) training framework, leveraging reinforcement learning to enhance the factuality and honesty of LLMs. Our experiments across multiple models show that RLKF training effectively enhances the ability of models to utilize their internal knowledge state, boosting performance in a variety of knowledge-based and honesty-related tasks.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Transformers represent belief state geometry in their residual stream
papers.research_question: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Specifically, is the structure given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process, and are belief states linearly represented in the residual stream?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical framework and empirical evidence that transformers trained on next-token prediction linearly represent the geometry of belief states (from the mixed-state presentation of the data-generating process) in their residual stream, even for complex fractal geometries, and that this representation captures information beyond local next-token predictions.
papers.conclusion: Transformers construct predictive representations that encode the complex geometry of belief updating over hidden states, capturing an inference process over the underlying structure of the data-generating process, which provides a concrete link between training data structure and internal model representations.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on data from hidden Markov models (HMMs) linearly represent the belief state geometry of the mixed-state presentation in their residual stream, as verified by linear regression.
The belief state representation emerges during training and is not an artifact, as shown by controls including cross-validation and shuffling.
For processes where distinct belief states share the same next-token distribution (e.g., RRXOR), the belief state geometry is not well represented in the final layer alone but is distributed across multiple layers of the residual stream.
The representation captures information about the entire future distribution, not just the next token, as demonstrated by comparing pairwise distances between belief states versus next-token probabilities.
The belief state geometry is robust to the choice of using pre- or post-layer normalization activations.
papers.limitation:
Experimental validation focused on small-scale systems (HMMs with 3-5 states and vocabularies of 2-3 tokens), a significant simplification compared to modern language models.
For realistic systems, the dimensionality of the belief state simplex would exceed the residual stream dimension, suggesting representation must be compressed; the nature of this compression is not understood.
Explicitly computing ground-truth belief states becomes intractable as the size of the minimal generating structure and context window length grows, requiring new methodologies for validation in larger settings.
The work is limited to the stationary ergodic setting, though the framework is expected to extend to non-stationary and non-ergodic processes.
The paper establishes the representation of belief states but does not test whether transformers implement a circuit for performing Bayesian updates.
future_direction: Extending the framework to non-stationary and non-ergodic processes, such as in-context learning.
Understanding how belief state geometry is compressed when the simplex dimension exceeds the residual stream dimension.
Investigating the mapping between belief states and features, which is likely complex and architecture-dependent.
papers.abstract: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Here, we present evidence that this structure is given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process. Leveraging the theory of optimal prediction, we anticipate and then find that belief states are linearly represented in the residual stream of transformers, even in cases where the predicted belief state geometry has highly nontrivial fractal structure. We investigate cases where the belief state geometry is represented in the final residual stream or distributed across the residual streams of multiple layers, providing a framework to explain these observations. Furthermore we demonstrate that the inferred belief states contain information about the entire future, beyond the local next-token prediction that the transformers are explicitly trained on. Our work provides a general framework connecting the structure of training data to the geometric structure of activations inside transformers.

papers.title: Can RNNs learn Recursive Nested Subject-Verb Agreements?
papers.research_question: Can recurrent neural networks (RNNs) learn recursive nested subject-verb agreements, and how do they represent such structures internally?
papers.core_contribution: RNNs do not learn systematic recursive rules for nested subject-verb agreement but show bounded generalization with primacy and recency effects, and a single unit can encode multiple grammatical numbers.
papers.conclusion: RNNs do not learn systematic recursive rules but approximate nested structures with bounded mechanisms, showing similarities to human cognitive limitations in processing center-embedded sentences.
papers.key_findings:
RNNs generalize to longer subject-verb dependencies but not to deeper tree structures.
LSTM-based models exhibit primacy and recency effects, performing well on outer- and innermost verbs but poorly on middle verbs.
Ablation studies show that a single unit can encode grammatical number for multiple nouns and its ablation dramatically affects performance on outer dependencies.
All tested RNN types, including those with structural bias (ON-LSTM, stack-RNNs, stack-LSTMs), fail to generalize to deeper structures.
Internal dynamics of key units reveal a fractal-like encoding that may implement a memory stack.
future_direction: Explore the similarity between RNN generalization patterns and human cognitive patterns in processing nested structures.
papers.abstract: One of the fundamental principles of contemporary linguistics states that language processing requires the ability to extract recursively nested tree structures. However, it remains unclear whether and how this code could be implemented in neural circuits. Recent advances in Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), which achieve near-human performance in some language tasks, provide a compelling model to address such questions. Here, we present a new framework to study recursive processing in RNNs, using subject-verb agreement as a probe into the representations of the neural network. We trained six distinct types of RNNs on a simplified probabilistic context-free grammar designed to independently manipulate the length of a sentence and the depth of its syntactic tree. All RNNs generalized to subject-verb dependencies longer than those seen during training. However, none systematically generalized to deeper tree structures, even those with a structural bias towards learning nested tree (i.e., stack-RNNs). In addition, our analyses revealed primacy and recency effects in the generalization patterns of LSTM-based models, showing that these models tend to perform well on the outer- and innermost parts of a center-embedded tree structure, but poorly on its middle levels. Finally, probing the internal states of the model during the processing of sentences with nested tree structures, we found a complex encoding of grammatical agreement information (e.g. grammatical number), in which all the information for multiple words nouns was carried by a single unit. Taken together, these results indicate how neural networks may extract bounded nested tree structures, without learning a systematic recursive rule.

papers.title: Rigorously Assessing Natural Language Explanations of Neurons
papers.research_question: How can we rigorously evaluate the faithfulness of natural language explanations that claim individual neurons in a language model represent a concept?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a framework with observational and intervention modes to evaluate natural language explanations of neurons, and applies it to show that GPT-4-generated explanations for GPT-2 XL neurons have low faithfulness and causal efficacy.
papers.conclusion: Natural language may not be the best medium for model explanations due to vagueness and ambiguity, and neurons may not be the optimal unit of analysis; structured formalisms and analysis of neuron groups are promising alternatives.
papers.key_findings:
Even among the top 0.6% of neurons with GPT-4 explanation scores ≥0.8, explanations achieve only 0.64 precision and 0.50 recall.
Intervention-based evaluation shows GPT-4 explanations have little to no causal efficacy, performing similarly to random baselines.
Individual neurons are not effective causal mediators; causal effects require aggregating over many neurons, especially in early MLP layers.
Natural language explanations are often vague and ambiguous, making them unreliable for technical decision-making.
The GPT-4 score used by Bills et al. (2023) is insensitive to Type I errors and does not guarantee faithful explanations.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is primarily on GPT-2 XL; results may not extend directly to other architectures.
Faithful explanations could be used for malicious manipulations of models.
future_direction: Use structured formalisms (e.g., programming languages) instead of natural language for explanations.
Analyze groups of neurons or other network components (e.g., attention heads, residual streams) as units of analysis.
Conduct similar evaluations on other model architectures.
papers.abstract: Natural language is an appealing medium for explaining how large language models process and store information, but evaluating the faithfulness of such explanations is challenging. To help address this, we develop two modes of evaluation for natural language explanations that claim individual neurons represent a concept in a text input. In the *observational mode*, we evaluate claims that a neuron a activates on all and only input strings that refer to a concept picked out by the proposed explanation E. In the *intervention mode*, we construe E as a claim that neuron a is a causal mediator of the concept denoted by E. We apply our framework to the GPT-4-generated explanations of GPT-2 XL neurons of Bills et al. (2023) and show that even the most confident explanations have high error rates and little to no causal efficacy. We close the paper by critically assessing whether natural language is a good choice for explanations and whether neurons are the best level of analysis.

papers.title: Surgical Activation Steering via Generative Causal Mediation
papers.research_question: Where should we intervene in a language model (LM) to localize and control behaviors that are diffused across many tokens of a long-form response?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Generative Causal Mediation (GCM), a method for selecting attention heads that are causal mediators of a target concept using contrastive long-form responses, enabling effective localization and steering of diffuse behaviors.
papers.conclusion: GCM provides an effective approach for localizing from and controlling the long-form responses of LMs.
papers.key_findings:
GCM successfully localizes concepts expressed in long-form responses and outperforms correlational probe-based baselines when steering with a sparse set of attention heads.
GCM variants (activation patching, attribution patching, attention head knockouts) provide effective strategies for concept localization.
Steering success depends on hyperparameters like the steering factor (α) and the percentage of heads intervened on (k).
Representation Fine-Tuning (ReFT) is an effective supervised steering method when combined with GCM localization.
papers.limitation:
Activation patching is computationally expensive, scaling linearly with the number of neurons.
Attribution patching is a linear approximation that may not be perfect, especially at the first and last layers.
future_direction: Extending GCM to other model components beyond attention heads.
Applying GCM to a broader range of tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: Where should we intervene in a language model (LM) to control behaviors that are diffused across many tokens of a long-form response? We introduce Generative Causal Mediation (GCM), a procedure for selecting model components, e.g., attention heads, to steer a binary concept (e.g., talk in verse vs. talk in prose) from contrastive long-form responses. In GCM, we first construct a dataset of contrasting inputs and responses. Then, we quantify how individual model components mediate the contrastive concept and select the strongest mediators for steering. We evaluate GCM on three tasks--refusal, sycophancy, and style transfer--across three language models. GCM successfully localizes concepts expressed in long-form responses and consistently outperforms correlational probe-based baselines when steering with a sparse set of attention heads. Together, these results demonstrate that GCM provides an effective approach for localizing and controlling the long-form responses of LMs.

papers.title: Interpreting the Repeated Token Phenomenon in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models fail to accurately repeat a single word when prompted, and how is this linked to the attention sink phenomenon?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a mechanistic explanation for repeated token divergence in LLMs by linking it to attention sinks, identifies the responsible neural circuit, and proposes a targeted patch to mitigate the vulnerability without impacting overall performance.
papers.conclusion: The study links repeated token divergence to attention sinks via neural circuits, shows how first layer confusion leads to divergence, and demonstrates a mitigation patch that addresses the vulnerability while preserving model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated token divergence is caused by the attention sink mechanism, where the first token receives disproportionately high attention.
The first attention layer marks the first token, but fails to distinguish it from repeated tokens, leading to confusion.
Specific MLP neurons (sink neurons) amplify hidden states for attention sinks, and are also activated by repeated tokens.
A 'cluster attack' extends the vulnerability to similar tokens without exact repetition, bypassing surface-level defenses.
A targeted patch that modifies sink neuron activations effectively mitigates the divergence without significant performance loss on other tasks.
papers.limitation:
The mechanism by which training data leakage occurs through attention sinks remains unclear.
The first attention layer's behavior was unique to LLaMa2, highlighting model-specific details.
The efficacy of token repetition in inducing sinks varies across models.
Not all tokens in LLaMa2 induce attention sinks.
Due to difficulty in assessing training data leakage, the success rate of the cluster attack was not quantified.
The mitigation strategy does not fully address the inherent vulnerability of causally masked Transformers to repeated tokens.
future_direction: Investigate broader generalizability of the findings across more models.
Explain why repeated token sequences lead to training data extraction.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their impressive capabilities, often fail to accurately repeat a single word when prompted to, and instead output unrelated text. This unexplained failure mode represents a vulnerability, allowing even end-users to diverge models away from their intended behavior. We aim to explain the causes for this phenomenon and link it to the concept of ``attention sinks'', an emergent LLM behavior crucial for fluency, in which the initial token receives disproportionately high attention scores. Our investigation identifies the neural circuit responsible for attention sinks and shows how long repetitions disrupt this circuit. We extend this finding to other non-repeating sequences that exhibit similar circuit disruptions. To address this, we propose a targeted patch that effectively resolves the issue without negatively impacting the model's overall performance. This study provides a mechanistic explanation for an LLM vulnerability, demonstrating how interpretability can diagnose and address issues, and offering insights that pave the way for more secure and reliable models.

papers.title: Emergent Structured Representations Support Flexible In-Context Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether large language models functionally rely on structured, human-like conceptual representations for reasoning during in-context concept inference.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs dynamically construct and use a structured, latent conceptual subspace during in-context inference, and this subspace is causally involved in predictions.
papers.conclusion: LLMs construct and use abstract structured representations for in-context inference, offering a mechanistic window into the computational basis of their adaptive behavior.
papers.key_findings:
A conceptual subspace emerges in middle to late layers, with persistent structure across contexts.
Causal mediation analysis shows this subspace is functionally central to model predictions.
Attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace.
The subspace becomes more stable with increasing numbers of demonstrations.
The subspace supports cross-context generalization via a functionally aligned relational structure.
papers.limitation:
Smaller models rely less consistently on the subspace mechanism, exhibiting more diffuse, non-subspace-specific strategies.
Findings are based on a specific reverse dictionary task and may not generalize to all reasoning contexts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit emergent behaviors suggestive of human-like reasoning. While recent work has identified structured, human-like conceptual representations within these models, it remains unclear whether they functionally rely on such representations for reasoning. Here we investigate the internal processing of LLMs during in-context concept inference. Our results reveal a conceptual subspace emerging in middle to late layers, whose representational structure persists across contexts. Using causal mediation analyses, we demonstrate that this subspace is not merely an epiphenomenon but is functionally central to model predictions, establishing its causal role in inference. We further identify a layer-wise progression where attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace, which is subsequently leveraged by later layers to generate predictions. Together, these findings provide evidence that LLMs dynamically construct and use structured, latent representations in context for inference, offering insights into the computational processes underlying flexible adaptation.

papers.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
papers.research_question: How can polysemantic interference structures in language models be exploited to manipulate model outputs, and do these interference patterns transfer across models of different scales and families?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that polysemantic interference structures in language models create a systematic vulnerability, and that interventions based on these structures, identified in small models, can transfer to larger instruction-tuned models for predictable behavioral control without requiring access to their internals.
papers.conclusion: Polysemantic interference reveals a systematic vulnerability in language models, and the generalization of these structures across scale and family challenges the view of polysemanticity as purely stochastic, offering new avenues for black-box control and theoretical insight into internal representation.
papers.key_findings:
Interventions leveraging polysemantic structures (feature-direction steering, token-gradient steering, prompt injection) can effectively manipulate model next-token predictions.
Polysemantic interference patterns are persistent across models: interventions distilled from small models (Pythia-70M, GPT-2-Small) transfer reliably to larger models (Llama-3.1, Gemma-2).
Many counterintuitive interference patterns are stable across models but remain largely opaque to human interpretation, suggesting models learn robust regularities not aligned with surface semantics.
Highly polysemantic neurons are more vulnerable to interventions; amplifying 'super-neurons' (activated by many features) strongly alters model behavior, while deactivating them has a reduced effect.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) whose outputs fluctuate with dimensionality and hyperparameters, yielding unstable features.
Interventions steer only one interference feature in one layer, while multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations could amplify and better obscure the effect.
Vulnerability is quantified solely via shifts in immediate next-token probabilities on two small base models, with only coarse transfer checks on larger instructed models.
future_direction: Establishing how these interventions alter non-trivial downstream tasks in bigger models.
Exploring multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations to amplify and better obscure intervention effects.
papers.abstract: Polysemanticity is pervasive in language models and remains a major challenge for interpretation and model behavioral control. Leveraging sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we map the polysemantic topology of two small models (Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small) to identify SAE feature pairs that are semantically unrelated yet exhibit interference within models. We intervene at four loci (prompt, token, feature, neuron) and measure induced shifts in the next-token prediction distribution, uncovering polysemantic structures that expose a systematic vulnerability in these models. Critically, interventions distilled from counterintuitive interference patterns shared by two small models transfer reliably to larger instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct), yielding predictable behavioral shifts without access to model internals. These findings challenge the view that polysemanticity is purely stochastic, demonstrating instead that interference structures generalize across scale and family. Such generalization suggests a convergent, higher-order organization of internal representations, which is only weakly aligned with intuition and structured by latent regularities, offering new possibilities for both black-box control and theoretical insight into human and artificial cognition.

papers.title: Too Big to Fool: Resisting Deception in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models of varying capacities within the same family balance in-context information against their internal world models, particularly when faced with intentionally misleading prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Larger language models exhibit greater resilience to deceptive prompts, demonstrating an advanced ability to integrate conflicting in-context information with their internal knowledge, without simply ignoring prompts or relying on memorization.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces an evaluation strategy that re-uses existing benchmarks with minimal changes to study LLM behavior. Experiments show that larger models are more resilient to deceptive prompts, indicating a better ability to integrate prompt information with internal knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models consistently show a smaller Relative Accuracy Drop when given deceptive hints, indicating higher resilience to misinformation.
Larger models do not ignore in-context information; they effectively follow legitimate instructions and utilize truthful hints.
The resilience is not due to memorization, as shown by control experiments with overfitted models and a model without prior exposure to the test data.
Larger models generally exhibit better instruction-following capabilities, except for the Gemma family which is an outlier.
Models can infer missing information from answer choices, maintaining accuracy above chance even when the question is removed.
papers.limitation:
The study focused exclusively on multiple-choice datasets, which may not capture nuances of open-ended or generative tasks.
Experiments involved only open-source LLMs, limiting generalizability to proprietary models with different architectures or training.
papers.abstract: Large language models must balance their weight-encoded knowledge with in-context information from prompts to generate accurate responses. This paper investigates this interplay by analyzing how models of varying capacities within the same family handle intentionally misleading in-context information. Our experiments demonstrate that larger models exhibit higher resilience to deceptive prompts, showcasing an advanced ability to interpret and integrate prompt information with their internal knowledge. Furthermore, we find that larger models outperform smaller ones in following legitimate instructions, indicating that their resilience is not due to disregarding in-context information. We also show that this phenomenon is likely not a result of memorization but stems from the models' ability to better leverage implicit task-relevant information from the prompt alongside their internally stored knowledge.

papers.title: Explainable AI for cyber threat Intelligence: Enhancing analyst trust
papers.research_question: How can Explainable AI (XAI) techniques improve analyst trust and decision-making in cyber threat intelligence systems?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that integrating Explainable AI (XAI) techniques like SHAP and LIME into cyber threat intelligence systems enhances analyst trust, reduces investigation time, and improves threat detection accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The integration of Explainable AI (XAI) into Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) systems represents a significant advancement in trust, transparency, and operational effectiveness, improving threat comprehension, reducing time-to-response, and fostering collaboration between human analysts and AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Integration of XAI techniques improved detection accuracy by 2.7% and reduced false positive rate by over 50%.
Analyst response time decreased by 31.5% when using XAI explanations.
Analyst trust scores increased by 45.8% with XAI-integrated systems.
XAI explanations, particularly SHAP and LIME, enhanced analyst comprehension and decision-making speed.
The study found that XAI fosters collaborative human-AI interaction in cybersecurity operations.
papers.limitation:
The experiment was limited to a synthetic environment and a single dataset.
Computational cost of XAI techniques like SHAP may not scale well in real-time environments.
Not all explanations were equally useful; effectiveness depends on user cognitive style and task context.
future_direction: Scalability and real-time constraints for XAI in high-speed SOC environments
Explainability in cyber-physical systems with hybrid XAI models
XAI for IoT and federated learning-based threat detection
papers.abstract: With the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) in the ecosystem of contemporary cyber threat intelligence (CTI) platforms, the issue of AI-driven decision interpretability and transparency has become increasingly common. Although there is an increased ability in machine learning models to detect the complex and evolving cyber threats, this usually prevents human trust and restricts perceived actionable insights because they are black boxed and have a challenge of accountability. This paper discusses the use of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI, including SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), LIME (Local interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations), and attention-based visualizations, in order to achieve better interpretability in CTI systems. We provide a case study illustrating that incorporation of XAI to threat detection pipelines enhances the analysis comprehension by analysts, saves investigation time, and enables informed decision-making within Security Operations Centers (SOCs). The evidence provided by our research indicates that XAI does not only make complex AI models understandable to human analysts yet can create a collaborative and transparent cybersecurity ecosystem. The study offers a viable system to implement XAI-enriched CTI that would enable more responsible and successful AI-empowered cybersecurity.

papers.title: Self-Detoxifying Language Models via Toxification Reversal
papers.research_question: How can pretrained language models be detoxified without fine-tuning or additional components by identifying and reversing the toxification direction in attention layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a lightweight method for language model detoxification that reverses the toxification direction in attention layers without fine-tuning, achieving comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods.
papers.conclusion: The method effectively detoxifies language models by manipulating attention layer information flow, providing a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning-based approaches.
papers.key_findings:
The method reduces toxicity effectively without fine-tuning, matching state-of-the-art performance.
Human evaluation shows it generates less toxic content while maintaining fluency and coherence.
Layer-wise ablation indicates that middle-upper attention layers are more critical for detoxification.
Adaptive scaling factors based on vector norms and similarities improve detoxification adaptability.
Logit lens analysis demonstrates suppression of toxic token probabilities in the residual stream.
papers.limitation:
The method's effectiveness depends on the model's pre-training knowledge and may not remove harmful content not associated with the prefix.
Full model access is required, making it unsuitable for API-only models.
papers.abstract: Language model detoxification aims to minimize the risk of generating offensive or harmful content in pretrained language models (PLMs) for safer deployment. Existing methods can be roughly categorized as finetuning-based and decoding-based. However, the former is often resource-intensive, while the latter relies on additional components and potentially compromises the generation fluency. In this paper, we propose a more lightweight approach that enables the PLM itself to achieve "self-detoxification". Our method is built upon the observation that prepending a negative steering prompt can effectively induce PLMs to generate toxic content. At the same time, we are inspired by the recent research in the interpretability field, which formulates the evolving contextualized representations within the PLM as an information stream facilitated by the attention layers. Drawing on this idea, we devise a method to identify the toxification direction from the normal generation process to the one prompted with the negative prefix, and then steer the generation to the reversed direction by manipulating the information movement within the attention layers. Experimental results show that our approach, without any fine-tuning or extra components, can achieve comparable performance with state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: Meaningless Tokens, Meaningful Gains: How Activation Shifts Enhance LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: Why does inserting meaningless tokens improve LLM reasoning performance, and how can this effect be harnessed?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic explanation for how meaningless tokens improve LLM reasoning via activation redistribution and introduces ARM, a lightweight inference-time method that reproduces this effect.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that activation redistribution is a key mechanism behind the meaningless-token effect and that ARM effectively harnesses this mechanism to improve LLM reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Inserting meaningless tokens induces an affine transformation on attention outputs, leading to activation redistribution in MLP layers.
Activation redistribution reduces near-zero activations and increases variance, enhancing the model's representational capacity for reasoning.
The proposed ARM method adaptively shifts near-zero activations outward, improving reasoning performance without changing input tokens.
ARM consistently improves performance across diverse models and reasoning benchmarks while being simple to implement.
papers.limitation:
Our method is primarily evaluated on reasoning tasks; its effectiveness on non-reasoning tasks is limited.
The hyperparameters of ARM need to be tuned per model family.
future_direction: Extending ARM to more layers or combining it with other inference-time optimizations.
Exploring the effect on non-reasoning tasks and automatic hyperparameter tuning.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the puzzling observation that inserting long sequences of meaningless tokens before the query prompt can consistently enhance LLM reasoning performance, this work analyzes the underlying mechanism driving this phenomenon and based on these insights proposes a more principled method that allows for similar performance gains. First, we find that the improvements arise from a redistribution of activations in the LLM's MLP layers, where near zero activations become less frequent while large magnitude activations increase. This redistribution enhances the model's representational capacity by suppressing weak signals and promoting stronger, more informative ones. Building on this insight, we propose the Activation Redistribution Module (ARM), a lightweight inference-time technique that modifies activations directly without altering the input sequence. ARM adaptively identifies near-zero activations after the non-linear function and shifts them outward, implicitly reproducing the beneficial effects of meaningless tokens in a controlled manner. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and model architectures clearly show that ARM consistently improves LLM performance on reasoning tasks while requiring only a few lines of simple code to implement. Our findings deliver both a clear mechanistic explanation for the unexpected benefits of meaningless tokens and a simple yet effective technique that harnesses activation redistribution to further improve LLM performance.

papers.title: Probing Latent Subspaces in LLM for AI Security: Identifying and Manipulating Adversarial States
papers.research_question: Can latent subspaces in LLMs be identified and manipulated to induce state transitions from safe to jailbroken states?
papers.core_contribution: This work demonstrates that latent subspaces in LLMs can be identified and manipulated to induce state transitions from safe to jailbroken states using LDA and targeted perturbations, paving the way for potential proactive defenses.
papers.conclusion: The methodology demonstrates the feasibility of using latent representations to manipulate model states and provides insights into attractor dynamics in LLMs, with potential for preemptive AI security.
papers.key_findings:
Last-token activations encode information about the model's state (safe vs jailbreak) and can be classified with above-chance accuracy.
Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) can separate safe and jailbreak activations into distinct latent subspaces, and a direction vector can be derived.
Applying the derived perturbation vector to safe activations can induce jailbreak responses in a subset of prompts (11% for Llama-3.1-8B, 13.39% for Qwen2.5-3B).
Targeted perturbations induce distinct downstream state changes that propagate through layers, while random perturbations do not.
The effect of targeted perturbation varies across layers, with middle layers (6-18) showing sustained effects, suggesting they may be critical for safety.
papers.limitation:
The perturbation vector was derived from a dataset of malicious cybersecurity-related prompt-injects, so the discovered subspace may reflect features specific to this domain.
Perturbations led to jailbreak transitions in only about 11% of tested prompts, indicating a low success rate.
The external evaluation performed by GPT-4o exhibited high variance in assigning labels to ambiguous outputs.
The method was developed and validated on decoder-only Transformers; generalizing to other LLM architectures requires further testing.
future_direction: Generalize the analysis by expanding the scope of malicious questions and prompt injects to multiple domains or adversarial content types.
Investigate stronger perturbation magnitudes without compromising the coherence of the LLM's response.
Test the methodology on other open-source and commercially available LLM architectures to confirm generalizability.
Incorporate additional rounds of assessment to mitigate label noise from external evaluators like GPT-4o.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various tasks, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial manipulations such as jailbreaking via prompt injection attacks. These attacks bypass safety mechanisms to generate restricted or harmful content. In this study, we investigated the underlying latent subspaces of safe and jailbroken states by extracting hidden activations from a LLM. Inspired by attractor dynamics in neuroscience, we hypothesized that LLM activations settle into semi stable states that can be identified and perturbed to induce state transitions. Using dimensionality reduction techniques, we projected activations from safe and jailbroken responses to reveal latent subspaces in lower dimensional spaces. We then derived a perturbation vector that when applied to safe representations, shifted the model towards a jailbreak state. Our results demonstrate that this causal intervention results in statistically significant jailbreak responses in a subset of prompts. Next, we probed how these perturbations propagate through the model's layers, testing whether the induced state change remains localized or cascades throughout the network. Our findings indicate that targeted perturbations induced distinct shifts in activations and model responses. Our approach paves the way for potential proactive defenses, shifting from traditional guardrail based methods to preemptive, model agnostic techniques that neutralize adversarial states at the representation level.

papers.title: Function Vectors in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does there exist a compact vector representation of an input-output function (function vector) in transformer language models that can be extracted and used to trigger the task in various contexts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that compact vector representations of input-output functions (function vectors) exist in transformer language models and can be extracted via causal mediation analysis; these vectors robustly trigger the corresponding tasks even in zero-shot and natural text contexts.
papers.conclusion: Function vectors are a compact internal representation of functions in large language models that can be extracted and used to trigger tasks robustly across contexts, and they exhibit compositional properties.
papers.key_findings:
Function vectors can be extracted from a small set of attention heads via causal mediation analysis.
FVs are portable across different contexts, including zero-shot and natural text settings.
FVs often encode the output vocabulary of the task but contain additional information beyond that.
FVs can be composed via vector algebra to create new function vectors for combined tasks.
The causal effect of FVs is strongest when added to middle layers of the network.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to relatively simple functions.
The conditions under which FVs can be composed are not fully characterized.
The extraction method relies on having a set of exemplars for the task.
future_direction: Investigate more complex functions.
Explore the relationship between FVs and other internal representations.
Use FVs for model editing and control.
papers.abstract: We report the presence of a simple neural mechanism that represents an input-output function as a vector within autoregressive transformer language models (LMs). Using causal mediation analysis on a diverse range of in-context-learning (ICL) tasks, we find that a small number attention heads transport a compact representation of the demonstrated task, which we call a function vector (FV). FVs are robust to changes in context, i.e., they trigger execution of the task on inputs such as zero-shot and natural text settings that do not resemble the ICL contexts from which they are collected. We test FVs across a range of tasks, models, and layers and find strong causal effects across settings in middle layers. We investigate the internal structure of FVs and find while that they often contain information that encodes the output space of the function, this information alone is not sufficient to reconstruct an FV. Finally, we test semantic vector composition in FVs, and find that to some extent they can be summed to create vectors that trigger new complex tasks. Our findings show that compact, causal internal vector representations of function abstractions can be explicitly extracted from LLMs. Our code and data are available at https://functions.baulab.info.

papers.title: SOM Directions are Better than One: Multi-Directional Refusal Suppression in Language Models
papers.research_question: Is refusal behavior in language models better represented by a single linear direction or by a low-dimensional manifold of multiple directions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a multi-directional approach using Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) to model refusal as a manifold, showing that ablating multiple directions is more effective for refusal suppression than ablating a single direction.
papers.conclusion: Modeling refusal as a manifold spanned by multiple, closely related directions provides a more faithful and effective view of safety-related behaviors in LLMs than the single-direction perspective.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating multiple refusal directions identified by SOMs (MD) significantly outperforms the single-direction baseline (SD) and other jailbreak algorithms (GCG, SAA) in terms of Attack Success Rate (ASR).
Ablating multiple directions compresses the variance of harmful prompt representations and shifts them closer to harmless representations in the model's activation space.
The multiple directions extracted by SOMs are closely related (non-orthogonal), suggesting refusal is encoded as a manifold rather than a set of orthogonal components.
The method is effective even against a model with a defense mechanism (Mistral-7B-RR).
The effectiveness of refusal suppression generally increases with the number of ablated directions (k).
papers.limitation:
The Bayesian Optimization search for the best combination of directions can require a high number of trials as the search space grows, impacting scalability and speed.
The method computes directions at a single layer and applies ablation uniformly across all layers, potentially missing layer-specific variations in refusal encoding.
future_direction: Explore more efficient or structured search strategies, gradient-based optimization, or pruning algorithms to improve the scalability of the direction search.
Investigate layer-specific directions and ablation strategies to better capture refusal encoding across different layers.
Investigate the effectiveness of training separate SOMs for harmless prompts instead of using a single centroid.
papers.abstract: Refusal refers to the functional behavior enabling safety-aligned language models to reject harmful or unethical prompts. Following the growing scientific interest in mechanistic interpretability, recent work encoded refusal behavior as a single direction in the model's latent space; e.g., computed as the difference between the centroids of harmful and harmless prompt representations. However, emerging evidence suggests that concepts in LLMs often appear to be encoded as a low-dimensional manifold embedded in the high-dimensional latent space. Motivated by these findings, we propose a novel method leveraging Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) to extract multiple refusal directions. To this end, we first prove that SOMs generalize the prior work's difference-in-means technique. We then train SOMs on harmful prompt representations to identify multiple neurons. By subtracting the centroid of harmless representations from each neuron, we derive a set of multiple directions expressing the refusal concept. We validate our method on an extensive experimental setup, demonstrating that ablating multiple directions from models' internals outperforms not only the single-direction baseline but also specialized jailbreak algorithms, leading to an effective suppression of refusal. Finally, we conclude by analyzing the mechanistic implications of our approach.

papers.title: Detoxifying Large Language Models via Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: Can knowledge editing techniques be used to detoxify Large Language Models (LLMs) by precisely modifying toxic regions?
papers.core_contribution: This paper constructs a comprehensive benchmark SafeEdit for detoxification evaluation and proposes a knowledge editing method DINM that can detoxify LLMs efficiently with a single instance by locating and editing toxic regions.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge editing, particularly the proposed DINM method, is a promising approach for detoxifying LLMs efficiently with good generalization, providing insights into underlying mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge editing exhibits potential ability to detoxify LLMs with limited impact on general performance.
DINM demonstrates stronger detoxifying performance with better generalization, significantly increasing detoxification success rates.
Toxic regions location plays a significant role in detoxification.
DINM attempts to erase toxic regions of LLM, while DPO and SFT bypass toxic regions.
Editing one instance can generalize to various unsafe categories, indicating shared toxic regions.
papers.limitation:
DINM may compromise general abilities, with observed declines in knowledge question answering and repetitive text generation.
There is significant performance variance when using different instances for editing, indicating sensitivity to the editing instance.
future_direction: Developing improved detoxifying approaches based on insights from internal mechanisms.
Further exploration of knowledge editing for safety and underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates using knowledge editing techniques to detoxify Large Language Models (LLMs). We construct a benchmark, SafeEdit, which covers nine unsafe categories with various powerful attack prompts and equips comprehensive metrics for systematic evaluation. We conduct experiments with several knowledge editing approaches, indicating that knowledge editing has the potential to detoxify LLMs with a limited impact on general performance efficiently. Then, we propose a simple yet effective baseline, dubbed Detoxifying with Intraoperative Neural Monitoring (DINM), to diminish the toxicity of LLMs within a few tuning steps via only one instance. We further provide an in-depth analysis of the internal mechanism for various detoxifying approaches, demonstrating that previous methods like SFT and DPO may merely suppress the activations of toxic parameters, while DINM mitigates the toxicity of the toxic parameters to a certain extent, making permanent adjustments. We hope that these insights could shed light on future work of developing detoxifying approaches and the underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/zjunlp/EasyEdit.

papers.title: What does the Knowledge Neuron Thesis Have to do with Knowledge?
papers.research_question: Does the Knowledge Neuron Thesis adequately explain the process of factual expression in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The Knowledge Neuron Thesis is an oversimplification; MLP weights store complex token expression patterns that are linguistically interpretable but do not constitute 'knowledge'.
papers.conclusion: The Knowledge Neuron Thesis is an oversimplification; MLP neurons store interpretable token expression patterns, not knowledge. A better understanding requires examining the entire transformer circuit, including attention mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Syntactic phenomena can be localized to specific neurons using the same gradient-based methods as factual knowledge.
Editing these identified neurons has limited impact on categorical predictions and is influenced by superficial cues like word co-occurrence frequencies.
The ROME model-editing method only superficially alters token association patterns and fails under newly proposed symmetry and synonymy criteria.
The distribution of knowledge neurons for syntactic and factual information is similar, with both occupying the topmost layers of the model.
MLP modules do not store knowledge but rather complex token expression patterns that can be interpreted linguistically.
papers.limitation:
Editing identified knowledge neurons has low reliability and is not strong enough to overturn categorical predictions.
Current circuit identification methods are ad hoc and have only been applied to a small set of tasks.
future_direction: Formalize the circuit interpretation framework and apply it to more tasks and phenomena.
Investigate the entire decision-making circuit beyond MLP modules.
papers.abstract: We reassess the Knowledge Neuron (KN) Thesis: an interpretation of the mechanism underlying the ability of large language models to recall facts from a training corpus.
